content.text:
Yes, there's one thing. **Sequencing lane lines up exactly with condition.** The filenames show that all three control samples (S1–S3) were sequenced on lane L002, and all three treated samples (S4–S6) on lane L001:

| Lane | Samples | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| L002 | S1, S2, S3 | control |
| L001 | S4, S5, S6 | treated |

This means the design can't separate the treatment effect from any lane effect, and adding lane to the model wouldn't fix it. A differential test of treated vs control is really a test of "treated *and* lane L001" vs "control *and* lane L002". Lanes on the same flowcell usually differ very little. If L001 and L002 come from different flowcells or sequencing runs, though, technical differences would show up as treatment effects. These files can't tell which case applies. The sequencing facility, or the run metadata you have, can.

Apart from that, the design is simple: 3 control vs 3 treated, one sample per replicate, one lane per sample, nothing excluded. With three replicates per group, the test can only detect fairly large or consistent effects. Missing a gene doesn't mean it's unaffected.

The validator passed this design because it checks structure, not confounding. Nothing has been changed. The samplesheet is written, and I'm waiting for you to say you're ready to start stage 02 for rnaseq_bulk.
